hints: Focus on what concentrated sulfuric acid tells you, it is a strong oxidiser that is only reduced by good reducing agents.
Recall the reducing power trend down Group 17, iodide is the strongest reducer and reduces sulfur from +6 all the way to -2 in H2S, while chloride cannot reduce it at all.
Use your identified X and Y to test reducing strength against bromine and solubility of their silver halides, remembering that a stronger reducer displaces a weaker one.
walkthrough:
**Identify X from the H2S clue**

Think like a detective. Concentrated sulfuric acid has sulfur in oxidation state +6. In $\text{H}_2\text{S}$ sulfur is -2.

That is a huge reduction of 8 electrons, so X must contain a very powerful reducing agent. Only iodide, $\text{I}^-$, is strong enough. So X is $\text{NaI}$.

**Identify Y from the no change clue**

For Y there is no change in sulfur oxidation number, so sulfuric acid is acting only as an acid, not as an oxidiser.

$$\text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{NaHSO}_4 + \text{HCl}$$
This is typical of chloride, $\text{Cl}^-$, which is too weak a reducer to reduce sulfur. So Y is $\text{NaCl}$.

**Check reducing power against bromine**

Reducing power increases down Group 17: $\text{Cl}^- < \text{Br}^- < \text{I}^-$. A stronger reducer will reduce the diatomic halogen of a weaker one.

$$2\text{I}^- + \text{Br}_2 \rightarrow \text{I}_2 + 2\text{Br}^-$$
So aqueous iodide (X) does reduce aqueous bromine. This confirms the correct statement.

options.A: X is NaI, so aqueous X contains I-. Iodide is a stronger reducing agent than bromide, so it reduces Br2 to Br- while being oxidised to I2. This matches the displacement trend.
options.B: Y is NaCl, so it gives white AgCl with AgNO3. AgCl dissolves in dilute aqueous ammonia and so is certainly soluble in concentrated ammonia. The precipitate insoluble in concentrated ammonia is AgI from X, not Y.
options.C: Only X (iodide) produces halogen I2 with concentrated H2SO4, alongside SO2, S and H2S. Y (chloride) produces only HCl gas with no oxidation change, so no Cl2 is formed.
options.D: Sulfur goes from +6 in H2SO4 to -2 in H2S, a gain of 8 electrons. Each I- to 1/2 I2 loses 1 electron, so 8 halide ions are needed, not 6. Six would be correct for reduction only to S (0) or for bromide reduction to SO2.
